full_text_en:
Chen Weihua v. Chengdu Computer Business Information Agency — copyright infringement dispute

Plaintiff: Chen Weihua, manager of Beijing Rongyida Electronics Co., Ltd.

Agent ad litem: Tian Yu, legal worker of Beijing Baocheng Legal Office.

Defendant: Chengdu Computer Business Information Agency.

Legal representative: Niu Bo, general manager.

Agent ad litem: Lu Junfeng, legal counsel of Chengdu Computer Business Information Agency.

Agent ad litem: Fang Fang, lawyer of Beijing Long'an Law Firm.

The plaintiff, Chen Weihua, filed a lawsuit with the Haidian District People's Court of Beijing against the defendant, Chengdu Computer Business Information Agency, over a copyright dispute.

The plaintiff alleged: On May 10, 1998, I wrote an article titled "A Playful Talk on MAYA" under the pen name "Wufang" and uploaded it to my personal homepage "3D Sesame Street," with the notation "Copyright reserved, Please do not reprint." On October 16 of the same year, the defendant, without my consent, published the article in the Home Edition of Issue No. 40 of its newspaper *Computer Business Information*. This act infringed my copyright. Therefore, I filed a lawsuit with the court, requesting that the defendant be ordered to publicly apologize, pay a manuscript fee of RMB 231, and pay punitive damages of RMB 50,000.

The defendant argued: The article "A Playful Talk on MAYA" was submitted by a reader via email to our agency's mailbox in August 1998. The email did not contain any statement such as "Copyright reserved, Please do not reprint." Our agency replied requesting the author's detailed information, but the recommender did not respond. On October 16 of the same year, we published the full text of the article in our newspaper, with the author credited as "Wufang," and also added an editor's note stating, "The origin of this article is as unknown as the 3D source in the text." We agree to pay the author of "A Playful Talk on MAYA" a manuscript fee of RMB 231 in accordance with the national manuscript fee standard, but request that the plaintiff prove that he is the author "Wufang." We have no subjective fault and our conduct does not constitute infringement, so we disagree with the apology and the claimed punitive damages.

The Haidian District People's Court of Beijing found the following facts upon trial:

"3D Sesame Street" is the name of a personal homepage on the Internet, with the URL "http://WWW.nease.net/~xmchang/3ds" (http://WWW3D.yeah.net), and the webmaster is credited as "Wufang." The homepage began uploading files in January 1998, primarily containing articles on three-dimensional animation design. On May 10 of the same year, an article titled "A Playful Talk on MAYA" was uploaded to the homepage, with the author credited as "Wufang." On October 16 of the same year, the defendant, Chengdu Computer Business Information Agency, published the article "A Playful Talk on MAYA" in its newspaper *Computer Business Information*. The article was credited to "Wufang," and the newspaper added an editor's note when publishing it, stating: "The origin of this text is as unknown as the 3D source in the article, but a loyal reader, 3D enthusiast and netizen strongly recommended it." Thereafter, the defendant retained a column for "Wufang" in its author database, noting only that the author's pen name was "Wufang," and recorded in the manuscript fee statistics table that the fee had not yet been paid. In November of the same year, the plaintiff, Chen Weihua, sent an email to the defendant stating that he was the author of "A Playful Talk on MAYA." On December 2 of the same year, the plaintiff sent a fax to the defendant claiming that the defendant should bear liability for infringement. After receiving the above correspondence, the defendant rejected the plaintiff's demands.

At present, there is no specific legal regulation governing the registration of personal homepages on the Internet in China. However, after a personal homepage is registered, the registrant obtains the account, password, and URL of the personal homepage. Under normal circumstances, the password of the personal homepage is held and used by its registrant, and the uploading and deletion of files are also performed by the registrant. During the trial, through on-site inspection, the plaintiff was able to modify the password of the personal homepage "3D Sesame Street" and upload or delete files; the article "A Playful Talk on MAYA" could be fixed on a computer hard drive and uploaded to the personal homepage of "Wufang" via a WWW server. The page of this article bore the notation "Copyright reserved, Please do not reprint." The defendant did not provide any contrary evidence to prove the existence of special circumstances or that the article "A Playful Talk on MAYA" had been published in a newspaper or periodical before being uploaded, nor did it provide original evidence of the reader's submission to it. Through court investigation, the defendant also acknowledged that the plaintiff was "Wufang."

The Haidian District People's Court of Beijing held that the infringement by the defendant, Chengdu Computer Business Information Agency, was established for the following reasons:

First, a work refers to an intellectual creation in the fields of literature, art, and science that is original and capable of being reproduced in a tangible form. Such intellectual creation should be capable of being fixed on a tangible medium for a certain period of time and maintained in a stable state, so as to be perceived or reproduced by the public directly or with the aid of a machine. The article "A Playful Talk on MAYA" involved in this case is a literary description of three-dimensional animation technology, possesses originality, can be fixed on a computer hard drive in digital form, uploaded to the Internet via a WWW server and maintained in a stable state, and can be accessed and reproduced by the public through networked computers. Therefore, this article is an intellectual labor achievement and should be regarded as a work protected by copyright law. Since there is no other evidence to prove that the article had been published before, the time of its first upload to the personal homepage "3D Sesame Street" shall be deemed as the time of publication.

Second, Chinese law provides that, in the absence of proof to the contrary, the person named on the work is the author. The webmaster of the personal homepage "3D Sesame Street" and the author of the article "A Playful Talk on MAYA" on that homepage are both named "Wufang." Although there are currently no clear legal provisions on the establishment and use of personal homepages, under normal circumstances, the modification of the password of a personal homepage and the addition or deletion of content can only be performed by the registrant of the personal homepage. The plaintiff, Chen Weihua, as a professional, was able to modify the password of the personal homepage and upload or delete files. The defendant, Chengdu Computer Business Information Agency, accordingly acknowledged that the plaintiff was "Wufang" and did not submit any contrary evidence to prove the existence of special circumstances. Therefore, Chen Weihua should be deemed as "Wufang," and the copyright of the article "A Playful Talk on MAYA" belongs to the plaintiff, Chen Weihua.

Third, copyright is the exclusive right granted by law to an author for his or her created work. The plaintiff, Chen Weihua, uploaded the article "A Playful Talk on MAYA" to the Internet for publication, which was essentially disseminating his work in cyberspace. The defendant, Chengdu Computer Business Information Agency, without authorization, published Chen Weihua's work "A Playful Talk on MAYA" in its newspaper which carries commercial advertisements, for its commercial purposes, thereby expanding the dissemination scope of the work and infringing upon the plaintiff's right to use the work and the right to receive remuneration. Therefore, the defendant shall bear liability for infringement in accordance with Article 46 of the Copyright Law of the People's Republic of China, cease the infringement, publicly apologize to the plaintiff, and compensate the plaintiff for the reasonable economic losses caused thereby. The defendant's argument that it had no subjective fault in using the work and therefore refused to bear infringement liability is inconsistent with the facts and lacks legal basis, and this court does not accept it.

Fourth, a party bears the burden of proof for its own claims. The plaintiff, Chen Weihua, requested the defendant, Chengdu Computer Business Information Agency, to pay punitive damages of RMB 50,000, but failed to provide corresponding evidence. In this regard, this court will determine the amount of compensation in accordance with the degree of infringement by the defendant and will not fully support the plaintiff's claim. In summary, the Haidian District People's Court of Beijing rendered the following judgment on April 28, 1999:

1. From the effective date of this judgment, the defendant, Chengdu Computer Business Information Agency, shall cease using the plaintiff Chen Weihua's work "A Playful Talk on MAYA."

2. Within fifteen days after the effective date of this judgment, the defendant, Chengdu Computer Business Information Agency, shall publish a statement in its newspaper *Computer Business Information* to publicly apologize to the plaintiff, Chen Weihua (the content of the apology must be reviewed by this collegiate bench). If the Chengdu Computer Business Information Agency refuses to perform this obligation, this court will publish the full text of the judgment in a nationally distributed professional newspaper, and the relevant costs shall be borne by the Chengdu Computer Business Information Agency.

3. Within ten days after the effective date of this judgment, the defendant, Chengdu Computer Business Information Agency, shall pay the plaintiff, Chen Weihua, a manuscript fee and compensation for economic losses totaling RMB 924.

The case acceptance fee of RMB 2,017 shall be borne by the defendant, Chengdu Computer Business Information Agency.

After the judgment was pronounced, both the plaintiff and the defendant accepted the judgment and did not appeal. The judgment has become legally effective.
